title: Franciscan Schoolmen
orientation: This chapter covers the Franciscan philosophical tradition that rivaled Dominican Thomism: Roger Bacon's encyclopedic proto-empiricism, Bonaventura's and Matthew of Aquasparta's Augustinian resistance to Aristotle, Duns Scotus's subtle realism, and William of Occam's logically rigorous nominalism and razor. It matters because Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology, and his political theory (developed with Marsiglio of Padua) of conciliar and popular sovereignty, mark a real turning point -- described by Russell as the last of the great scholastics and, through his influence on Luther and the conciliar movement, an anticipation of currents that fed into the Reformation.
historical_background: Franciscans were, on the whole, less strictly orthodox than Dominicans and did not accept Thomas Aquinas's authority; the order's leading philosophers -- Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, and William of Occam -- developed independently of, and often against, Thomistic Aristotelianism, generally retaining a larger admixture of Augustinian Platonism. The chapter's second half turns to Occam's involvement in the Franciscan poverty dispute with Pope John XXII, his exile (with Marsiglio of Padua) to the protection of Emperor Louis of Bavaria in Munich, and the broader fourteenth-century power realignment (Avignon papacy, Anglo-French war, the rise of conciliarism) within which his political writings must be understood.
philosophical_problems: Whether experiment and observation, rather than argument from authority, should be the primary source of knowledge (Roger Bacon)

The 'principle of individuation': what makes two individual things of the same species genuinely distinct from one another -- form (Duns Scotus) or spatial position in undifferentiated matter (Aquinas)?
Whether any sure and certain natural knowledge is possible without a special divine illumination (Duns Scotus)
Whether logic and the theory of knowledge can be pursued independently of metaphysics and theology (Occam)
The status of universals in logic versus in reality (Occam's nominalism)
Whether ultimate political authority in Church and State rests with the Pope/Emperor or with the community/General Council (Marsiglio, Occam)

philosophers_discussed.name: Roger Bacon
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Franciscan polymath (ca. 1214-ca.1294) valued experiment and mathematics, wrote Opus Majus/Minus/Tertium at the Pope's request while under a publication ban, was later imprisoned fourteen years by his own order for attacking clerical ignorance; encyclopedic but unsystematic, and, per Russell, not as purely 'scientific' as later reputation suggests.

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Bonaventura
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: General of the Franciscan order who forbade Bacon to publish; a follower of Anselm who upheld the ontological argument, saw Aristotelianism as fundamentally opposed to Christianity, and believed in Platonic ideas known perfectly only by God.

philosophers_discussed.name: Matthew of Aquasparta
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Follower of Bonaventura, more touched by the new Aristotelianism than his teacher; opposed Aquinas from an Augustinian standpoint while treating Aristotle as 'The Philosopher'; sought a middle way between Plato (wisdom without knowledge) and Aristotle (knowledge without wisdom).

philosophers_discussed.name: Duns Scotus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Continued the Franciscan controversy with Aquinas (ca. 1270-1308); defended the Immaculate Conception; held that sure natural knowledge requires divine illumination; a moderate realist who argued the 'principle of individuation' must be form, not matter, since being and essence do not differ -- a more Platonic position than Aquinas's.

philosophers_discussed.name: William of Occam
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's central figure (ca. 1290-1349/50), pupil then rival of Duns Scotus; involved in the Franciscan poverty controversy against Pope John XXII, exiled to Munich under Emperor Louis's protection; developed Occam's razor, a nominalist logic sharply separated from metaphysics and theology, and (with Marsiglio) an influential political theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty preferred by Luther among the schoolmen.

philosophers_discussed.name: Marsiglio of Padua
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Close friend of Occam whose political opinions he influenced; held that the legislator is the majority of the people, who have the right to punish princes and to exercise sovereignty over the Church (including the laity) through elected representatives to General Councils, with the Pope stripped of special powers.

philosophers_discussed.name: Dante
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A great poetic innovator but, as a political thinker, dated: his 'De Monarchia' argues Emperor and Pope are both independent and divinely appointed, a Ghibelline position Russell judges 'hopelessly out of date' by the time he wrote.

schools_discussed: Franciscan scholasticism (Augustinian/Platonist current, opposed to strict Thomism)
Averroism (referenced as background to Franciscan/Dominican disputes over the active intellect)
The conciliar movement (arguing General Councils hold authority over popes)

core_concepts.name: The principle of individuation (Duns Scotus vs. Aquinas)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: If two things belong to the same species (say, two people), what makes them two distinct individuals rather than one? Aquinas held that, for material things, two individuals of the same essence can be exactly alike in essence and differ only by occupying different positions in space (like identical twins). Duns Scotus disagreed: since he held being and essence are not really different, he concluded that if two things are genuinely distinct, they must differ by some qualitative difference of form, not merely by spatial position -- a view closer to Platonism than Aquinas's.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The scholastic problem of specifying what makes numerically distinct individual substances of the same species genuinely different from one another; Duns Scotus locates this in form/haecceity rather than, as Aquinas does for material substances, in differentiated spatial position within otherwise undifferentiated matter.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is a central node connecting medieval metaphysics to modern philosophy of identity; Russell traces its modernization through Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles and the subsequent critique of the very notion of 'substance.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Duns Scotus (ca. 1270-1308) in direct opposition to Aquinas's treatment of essential vs. accidental properties in individuation.
examples: Aquinas's view that identical twins could, in principle, differ solely by the spatial position of their otherwise identical bodies
Leibniz's later 'identity of indiscernibles,' restating the problem by replacing 'essence' with 'all true propositions about the thing'
objections: Physicists later objected to Leibniz's principle, arguing two particles of matter might differ solely in spatiotemporal position -- a view Russell notes relativity complicates further by reducing space and time to relations
competing_positions: Aquinas's view that pure matter consists of undifferentiated parts distinguished solely by spatial position
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell traces a direct modernizing lineage from Scotus's problem through Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles to the rejection of 'substance' altogether, at which point 'a thing' becomes a mere bundle of qualities -- a view Russell says is, in this later form, closer to Scotus than to Aquinas; Russell notes he treats a version of this question himself under 'Proper Names' in his own Inquiry into Meaning and Truth.

core_concepts.name: Occam's razor
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Occam is famous for a principle -- though not, Russell notes, in the exact wording usually attributed to him -- that we should not multiply entities beyond what is strictly necessary to explain the facts. If a phenomenon can be fully explained without assuming some extra hypothetical entity, there is no ground for assuming that entity exists.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The methodological principle, associated with (though not verbatim from) William of Occam, that explanations should not posit more entities than are necessary; often rendered 'Entities are not to be multiplied without necessity,' closer to Occam's actual formulation 'It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell states he has 'himself found this a most fruitful principle in logical analysis,' directly linking Occam's medieval logical practice to Russell's own twentieth-century philosophical method.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Attributed to William of Occam (ca. 1290-1349/50), though the exact phrase 'Entities are not to be multiplied without necessity' does not appear in his surviving works.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Explicitly endorsed and used by Russell in his own logical analysis; became a general methodological touchstone across later philosophy and science.

core_concepts.name: Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Occam argued logic should be treated as an independent tool for studying the natural world, not something that has to rest on metaphysical or theological commitments. Logic deals with 'terms' or concepts as meaningful, not with things themselves (which is the job of science) and not with psychological states. He distinguished 'terms of first intention' (which point at things, used in science) from 'terms of second intention' (which point at other terms, used in logic), with only six genuinely metaphysical terms (being, thing, something, one, true, good) that straddle both. On universals specifically, Occam agreed with Aquinas against Averroes, Avicenna, and the Augustinians that only individual things, minds, and acts of understanding really exist; universals are signs of many things, not things themselves.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Occam's methodological program, per the interpretation of Ernest Moody that Russell endorses, of restoring a purified Aristotelian logic as an independent instrument of natural philosophy, freed from the Augustinian and Arabic metaphysical/theological accretions that (via Porphyry's questions about genera and species) had entangled logic with metaphysics since late antiquity.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: By treating logic and empirical inquiry as autonomous from theology, Occam's approach, in Russell's (and Moody's) reading, encouraged scientific research rather than anticipating modern philosophy wholesale, correcting a common historiographical tendency to over-modernize him.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Occam at Oxford and Paris, drawing on Ernest E. Moody's interpretation in The Logic of William of Occam, which Russell explicitly follows and endorses over the more common view of Occam as a precursor of Descartes or Kant.
examples: Occam's fallacy warning: 'Man is a species, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is a species' -- confusing the word as thing with the word as meaning
The six purely metaphysical terms Occam allows (being, thing, something, one, true, good), predicable of each other but not required for logic proper
Occam's example that Socrates is similar to Plato, but not in virtue of a further 'thing' called similarity -- similarity is a term of second intention, existing in the mind
competing_positions: The Scotist/Augustinian tradition, which (following Porphyry's questions about the reality of genera and species) had made logic dependent on metaphysics and theology
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Occam's immediate follower Nicholas of Oresme applied this independent, non-dogmatic spirit to planetary theory, anticipating Copernicus by showing that both geocentric and heliocentric theories equally explain the facts known in his day, with no way then available to decide between them.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Occam holds that universals exist ante rem only in God's mind for the purpose of creation, a theological role Aquinas also accepts, but insists universals play no such role in explaining ordinary human knowledge (universale post rem only).

core_concepts.name: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Marsiglio of Padua argued that ultimate legislative authority belongs to the majority of the people, who have the right to punish even princes, and that this popular sovereignty extends to the Church too: local councils (including laypeople) should elect representatives to General Councils, which alone should have power to excommunicate and to authoritatively interpret Scripture, leaving the Pope with no special powers and no secular authority. Occam did not go quite as far as Marsiglio but worked out a fully democratic method for electing the General Council.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The fourteenth-century political theory, developed chiefly by Marsiglio of Padua and adopted in modified form by Occam, that legislative and even ecclesiastical authority derives from the sovereignty of the people (including the laity), to be exercised through elected representative councils rather than through unilateral papal or imperial authority.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It marks a shift from the earlier, purely imperial form of opposition to the papacy toward a genuinely democratic one, which Russell says 'ultimately led to the Reformation,' and it directly informed the conciliar movement that resolved the Great Schism in the following century (covered in Chapter XV).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Marsiglio of Padua (1270-1342) in close collaboration with Occam during their shared exile under the protection of Emperor Louis of Bavaria in Munich, following their excommunication in 1328.
examples: Occam's reported remark to the Emperor: 'Do you defend me with the sword, and I will defend you with the pen.'
Occam's 'Eight Questions Concerning the Power of the Pope,' addressing burning practical political questions of the day
competing_positions: Dante's De Monarchia, which held Emperor and Pope both independently divinely appointed -- a position Russell calls already outdated
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The conciliar movement it inspired healed the Great Schism at the Council of Constance (1414-18); Russell notes, however, that its aim (preserving Catholic unity through democratic means) differed from the later Protestant claim to private judgement, which rejected submission to any General Council; Occam was, of all the schoolmen, the one Luther preferred.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political-theological: Occam and Marsiglio were excommunicated in 1328 for siding with Michael of Cesena in the Franciscan poverty dispute against Pope John XXII.

arguments.title: Duns Scotus's argument that individuation is by form, not matter
premises: Being is not really different from essence

If two individual things of the same species could be exactly alike in essence, distinguished only by spatial position, this would require essence to be separable from the individuating factor in a way inconsistent with the being-essence identity
arguments.conclusion: Distinct individual things must always differ by some qualitative difference of form, not merely by position in undifferentiated matter.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as flowing directly from Scotus's more Platonic-leaning metaphysics (via Augustine), in contrast with Aquinas's view that material substances of the same species can be exactly alike in essence, differentiated solely by their spatial position.
objections: Aquinas's alternative, that pure matter consists of undifferentiated parts distinguished only by position, remains the competing scholastic view
implications: Anticipates, per Russell, the modern move (via Leibniz) toward defining individuality by the totality of true propositions about a thing rather than by a separate metaphysical 'essence'

arguments.title: Occam's resolution of the flatus-vocis/universals fallacy
premises: Terms of first intention point at things (used in science); terms of second intention point at other terms (used in logic)
'Man is a species' is not a proposition of science, because it requires only a knowledge of logic, not a knowledge of actual men
Failing to distinguish the word as thing from the word as meaning produces fallacies
arguments.conclusion: The syllogism 'Man is a species, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is a species' is fallacious because it illegitimately mixes first- and second-intention uses of 'man.'
arguments.explanation: This is Occam's worked example for why logic must carefully track the distinction between terms used to talk about things and terms used to talk about other terms, underwriting his broader separation of logic from metaphysics.
implications: Supports Occam's broader nominalist claim that only individual things, minds, and acts of understanding truly exist -- universals being merely signs predicable of many things, not things themselves

key_distinctions: Terms of first intention (pointing at things) vs. terms of second intention (pointing at other terms) -- Occam
Essential vs. accidental properties, and their bearing on the 'principle of individuation' -- Duns Scotus vs. Aquinas

Universale ante rem (in God's mind before creation, accepted by both Aquinas and Occam) vs. universale post rem (in the human mind after experience, the only kind Occam allows for explaining human knowledge)
Imperial-style opposition to the papacy (Dante) vs. democratic/conciliar opposition (Marsiglio, Occam)
Private judgement (later Protestant doctrine) vs. conciliar/democratic but still unity-preserving reform (Marsiglio's and Occam's actual position)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Duns Scotus's and Bonaventura's Augustinian Platonism continues the tradition traced from Saint Augustine and the School of Chartres in earlier chapters; Occam's critique of how Porphyry's ancient questions about genera and species (from his commentary on Aristotle's Categories) had entangled logic with metaphysics directly continues the problem of universals debated by Roscelin, William of Champeaux, and Abelard in Chapter XI, and by Avicenna in Chapter X.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell explicitly traces the principle of individuation forward to Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles and the subsequent critique of 'substance,' and states he treats a related question himself under 'Proper Names' in his own Inquiry into Meaning and Truth; Occam's political theory, via Luther's preference for him among the schoolmen, is presented as feeding into the Reformation, while the conciliar movement he helped inspire is picked up again in the following chapter.
political_social_context: The chapter situates Occam's political writings within the broader collapse of both imperial and papal authority: the Avignon papacy had made the Pope a political subordinate of the King of France, weakening papal claims to universal temporal authority just as French and English national strength eclipsed the Empire's; England's war with France (and consequent alliance with the Emperor) made England antipapal too, providing political cover for figures like Occam and, later, Wycliffe.
religion_science_culture_context: The Franciscan dispute with John XXII over the ownership of Church property (Occam and Michael of Cesena's excommunication in 1328) directly connects religious poverty ideals (introduced with Saint Francis in the previous chapter) to high medieval constitutional theory; Nicholas of Oresme's application of Occam's spirit of open inquiry to planetary theory is presented as a modest but real precursor to Copernican astronomy.
russell_presentation: Russell is notably deflationary about Roger Bacon's popular reputation, crediting his genuine value of experiment and his geographical influence on Columbus, but judging him 'not, to my mind, so scientific as is sometimes thought' and unsystematic despite his encyclopedic learning; he also flatly denies the popular claim that Bacon invented gunpowder. Russell treats Duns Scotus's metaphysics respectfully as a serious, more Platonic-leaning alternative to Aquinas on individuation, tracing its modern descendants carefully. His treatment of Occam is the chapter's most sympathetic: Russell explicitly follows Ernest Moody's revisionist interpretation over the common tendency to read Occam as a precursor of Descartes or Kant, praises Occam's razor as a principle Russell himself has found fruitful, and credits Occam's separation of logic from theology with encouraging scientific research. Russell's tone throughout combines historical caution (repeatedly correcting popular misattributions -- Occam's razor's exact wording, Bacon and gunpowder) with genuine philosophical engagement, particularly on individuation and Occam's logic.
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism: some historians of medieval philosophy have questioned Russell's heavy reliance on Ernest Moody's specific interpretation of Occam as 'restoring pure Aristotle' rather than innovating, arguing that Occam's nominalism and epistemology (e.g. his treatment of intuitive cognition and contingent propositions) had genuinely novel implications beyond a mere purification project, whatever Occam's own self-understanding.
key_takeaways: Franciscan philosophers (Bacon, Scotus, Occam) were generally less strictly Thomistic and retained more Augustinian/Platonist influence than Dominicans.
Roger Bacon valued experiment and mathematics highly but was, per Russell, encyclopedic rather than systematic, and less purely 'scientific' than his later reputation suggests.
Duns Scotus located the 'principle of individuation' in form rather than matter, a more Platonic position than Aquinas's, which Russell traces forward to Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles.
Occam's razor ('entities are not to be multiplied without necessity') is a methodological principle Russell himself endorses as fruitful for logical analysis.
Occam, following Moody's interpretation (endorsed by Russell), aimed to restore a pure, theologically independent Aristotelian logic rather than to anticipate modern philosophy.

Occam and Marsiglio of Padua developed an influential theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty over Church and State, later preferred by Luther among all the schoolmen and feeding into the conciliar movement that resolved the Great Schism.
study_notes:
This chapter rewards close comparison between the Franciscan and Dominican responses to Aristotle: while Aquinas (previous chapter) sought to fully naturalize Aristotle within Christian orthodoxy, the Franciscans here split into two camps -- Bonaventura and Matthew of Aquasparta, who kept Aristotle at arm's length in favor of Augustine and Plato, and Duns Scotus and Occam, who engaged more seriously and technically with Aristotelian logic but reached different metaphysical conclusions than Aquinas (on individuation) or pushed logic in a more independent, less metaphysically loaded direction (Occam).

The chapter's second half shifts from metaphysics/logic to political theory, and this shift is not incidental: Occam's involvement in the Franciscan poverty controversy directly caused his exile and turn to political writing, so his logical and political works, though topically distinct, share a common biographical origin. Pay attention to how Russell distinguishes Marsiglio's and Occam's conciliarism from later Protestant 'private judgement': both aimed at preserving a unified Catholic Church through more democratic, representative structures, not at legitimizing individual doctrinal dissent -- a distinction that matters for understanding why the conciliar movement (covered next chapter) ultimately subsided once it had resolved the Great Schism, rather than producing lasting constitutional reform of the papacy.

Finally, take note of Russell's explicit methodological self-placement: he credits Occam's razor as something he has personally found useful in his own logical analysis, one of the clearest moments in these chapters where Russell draws a direct line between a medieval scholastic tool and his own twentieth-century philosophical practice.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The principle that you shouldn't assume more things exist than you need to explain the facts.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A methodological principle associated with William of Occam (though not found verbatim in his works) holding that explanations should posit the fewest possible entities; closest to his own phrasing, 'It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.'
related_concepts: Terms of first and second intention

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Occam's distinction between words that point directly at things in the world (first intention) and words that point at other words or concepts (second intention).
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Occam's logic, terms of first intention signify things directly and belong to the sciences; terms of second intention signify other terms/concepts and belong to logic; confusing the two produces fallacies such as 'Socrates is a species.'
related_concepts: Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The question of what makes two individual things of the same kind actually two separate things rather than one.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The scholastic problem of identifying the metaphysical ground of numerical distinctness among individuals of a shared species or essence; Duns Scotus locates it in form, Aquinas (for material things) in differentiated spatial position within matter.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that a General Council of the Church, rather than the Pope alone, holds ultimate authority in matters of doctrine and Church governance.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The theory, developed by Marsiglio of Padua and adopted in modified form by Occam, that supreme ecclesiastical authority (including the power to excommunicate and authoritatively interpret Scripture) belongs to a representative General Council rather than to the Pope alone.
related_concepts: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Latin terms for 'universal before the thing' (an idea in God's mind before creation) and 'universal after the thing' (a general concept formed in the human mind after experiencing many particular things).
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Scholastic terms (introduced fully in Chapter X via Avicenna) distinguishing universals as they exist in the divine mind prior to creation from universals as abstracted human concepts; Occam accepts the former only for explaining creation, not for explaining ordinary human knowledge, where only the post rem sense applies.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, was Roger Bacon 'praised far beyond his deserts' in modern times?
questions.answer: Though Bacon genuinely valued experiment and mathematics and wrote perceptively on geography (influencing Columbus), his learning was encyclopedic rather than systematic, he had little actual influence in his own time, and Russell judges him 'not, to my mind, so scientific as is sometimes thought.' Russell also debunks the popular English claim that Bacon invented gunpowder.
questions.explanation: This is a clear instance of Russell correcting an inflated popular reputation against the chapter's own textual evidence.

questions.prompt: Compare Duns Scotus's and Aquinas's views on the 'principle of individuation.'
questions.answer: Aquinas holds that, for material substances, two individuals of the same species can be exactly alike in essence, differentiated solely by occupying different positions in otherwise undifferentiated matter. Duns Scotus, holding that being and essence are not really distinct, concludes instead that genuinely distinct individuals must always differ by some qualitative difference of form, a more Platonic-leaning position.
questions.explanation: Russell traces this disagreement forward to Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles as a modernized version of the same underlying problem.

questions.prompt: What is 'Occam's razor,' and in what form does it actually appear in Occam's own works according to Russell?
questions.answer: Occam's razor is the principle that entities should not be multiplied without necessity; Russell notes the exact phrase is not found in Occam's works, but that Occam did write something with much the same effect: 'It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.' Russell states he has personally found this principle fruitful in his own logical analysis.
questions.explanation: This is one of the clearest points where Russell links medieval scholastic method directly to his own philosophical practice.

questions.prompt: According to Moody's interpretation (endorsed by Russell), what was Occam actually trying to accomplish, as opposed to the common view of him as a precursor of modern philosophy?
questions.answer: Occam was mainly concerned to restore a pure Aristotle, freed from both Augustinian and Arabic (especially Porphyry-derived) influences that had entangled logic with metaphysics and theology -- a project also, to a considerable extent, shared by Aquinas, though the Franciscans had continued to follow Augustine more closely. Reading Occam as anticipating Descartes or Kant, Moody and Russell argue, is a historiographical mistake driven by the desire to find a smooth transition from scholastic to modern philosophy.
questions.explanation: This revisionist framing shapes Russell's entire presentation of Occam in this chapter.

questions.prompt: What events led to Occam's excommunication and exile, and where did he take refuge?
questions.answer: Occam, summoned to Avignon by Pope John XXII to answer heresy charges concerning transubstantiation, instead sided with Michael of Cesena (General of the Franciscan order) in the dispute over Franciscan ownership of property; Occam, Michael of Cesena, and Marsiglio of Padua were all excommunicated in 1328, escaped Avignon, and took refuge with Emperor Louis of Bavaria, eventually settling in Munich.
questions.explanation: This exile is the direct biographical context for Occam's political writings with Marsiglio.

questions.prompt: What political theory did Marsiglio of Padua develop, and how far did Occam follow him?
questions.answer: Marsiglio held that the legislator is the majority of the people, who have the right to punish princes, and that popular sovereignty extends to the Church, including the laity, through local councils electing representatives to General Councils, which alone should hold power to excommunicate and interpret Scripture, with no secular authority for the Church and no special powers for the Pope. Occam did not go quite as far as Marsiglio, but worked out a fully democratic method for electing the General Council.
questions.explanation: Russell notes this current of opposition to the Pope, unlike earlier purely imperial opposition, acquired a genuinely democratic character that ultimately fed into the Reformation.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Occam's example of a logical fallacy caused by confusing terms of first and second intention.
questions.answer: 'Man is a species, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is a species' is fallacious because 'Man is a species' uses 'man' as a term of second intention (a logical term about the concept 'man'), while 'Socrates is a man' uses 'man' as a term of first intention (predicating a real property of a real individual). The syllogism illegitimately treats these as the same use of 'man,' producing a nonsensical conclusion.
questions.explanation: This example grounds Occam's broader insistence on keeping logic (second intention) rigorously distinct from the sciences (first intention).

quiz.prompt: According to Ernest Moody's interpretation, which Russell endorses, what was Occam's actual philosophical project?
options: To anticipate Descartes's method of doubt
To restore a pure Aristotle, freed of Augustinian and Arabic accretions, rather than to found modern philosophy
To prove the existence of God more rigorously than Aquinas
To synthesize Plato and Aristotle completely
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly follows Moody's view that reading Occam as a precursor of Descartes or Kant is a historiographical mistake; Occam aimed to restore genuine Aristotelian logic.
quiz.related_concept: Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology

quiz.prompt: According to Marsiglio of Padua's political theory, who or what should hold ultimate power to excommunicate and interpret Scripture?
options: The General Council, elected via representatives from local councils including the laity
quiz.explanation: Marsiglio held that the General Council alone should have power to excommunicate and give authoritative interpretations of Scripture, with the Pope stripped of special powers.
quiz.related_concept: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty

quiz.prompt: Martin Luther, among all the medieval schoolmen, preferred William of Occam.
quiz.explanation: Russell states explicitly that 'of all the schoolmen, Occam was the one whom Luther preferred.'
quiz.related_concept: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Duns Scotus's and Aquinas's treatments of the 'principle of individuation,' and trace how Russell says the problem was later modernized by Leibniz.
rubric: States both Scotus's and Aquinas's positions accurately
Explains the role of the essence/being distinction in Scotus's argument
Traces the connection to Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain Occam's project of separating logic from metaphysics and theology, and assess why Russell considers this historically significant for the encouragement of scientific research.
rubric: Uses specific examples (e.g. the 'Socrates is a species' fallacy)
Connects the project to Nicholas of Oresme's planetary theory
Engages with Russell's and Moody's revisionist interpretation of Occam
